meta.date_display: the Fourteenth of November, Two Thousand and Twenty-Six

news.subhead: THE INK DESK: THE ANSWER ARRIVES FOUR DAYS EARLY — BAUERS, HERO OF THE LATE OCTOBER, TAKES EIGHT-AND-FIFTY MILLIONS OVER FOUR YEARS FROM THE CRIMSON HOSE, AND THE CHAMPIONS, WHO KNOW THIS RITUAL BY HEART, STAND TO POCKET A PREMIUM PICK FOR THEIR TROUBLE
news.body:
The answer was not due until Tuesday. The qualifying offer that Milwaukee tendered its first baseman carried a deadline of the 17th — an appointment this paper's ledger has kept all week — and Jake Bauers answered it four days early, in another club's ink. The Red Sox and the hero of the late October have agreed on a contract of four years and $58 million, pending a physical, the figures confirmed to MLB.com's Mark Feinsand after ESPN's Jeff Passan first carried the report: the largest signature of the young offseason, and the first of the winter's dominoes to fall with an audible report.[^browne][^espn-bauers] The purchase is Boston doctrine made flesh. Craig Breslow, the president of baseball operations, had lately observed that a club without obvious holes must be "open-minded, flexible and opportunistic" in its improving, and an attack that finished 26th in home runs and 20th in slugging has now bought itself the most patient bat on the open market.[^browne]

What the Fenway men are buying is a career year with the receipts to argue it no accident. Bauers, 30, batted .266 with a .389 on-base mark and a .484 slug across 578 plate appearances, struck a team-high 26 home runs and drove in 86; he walked at a 16.3 percent rate that stood in the 98th percentile of the league, and by the Statcast ledger he hit the ball harder than ever in his life — an average exit speed of 92.1 mph, a hard-hit rate of 51.9 percent, a barrel rate of 14 percent, every one of them above the 90th percentile — though the whiffs remain plentiful, his 27 percent strikeout rate being the price of the patience.[^browne] October wants no retelling in these columns, but shall have a little anyway: the 12-pitch walk that set up the second game's victory in the league championship set, the go-ahead clout off Blake Snell at the end of an 11-pitch audience in the third, the series' Most Valuable honor as the Suds men swept the two-time defending titleholders of Los Angeles — and a quiet Fall Classic that mattered not at all, his club winning it in five. Nor should the romance beneath the figures go unrecorded: after the 2024 season, when he batted .199, Bauers was minded to give the game up entirely, until his wife, Lauren, revealed she was expecting, and the man reconsidered. Two years from that crossroads he is a champion with $58 million in promised wages.[^browne] The fit at Boston is a winter's puzzle happily deferred — Willson Contreras keeps first base, the designated place is shared with Masataka Yoshida in the final year of his engagement — but the Monster's wall stands 310 feet from the plate, and Bauers' habit of taking his singles and doubles the other way will find it a friendly neighbor.[^browne]

And in Milwaukee, the ritual plays out precisely as the house has rehearsed it. Because the Cream City men extended their qualifying offer and the man signed elsewhere for more than $50 million, they stand to receive a compensation pick between the end of the first round and the start of Competitive Balance Round A in next summer's draft — the same toll collected when Willy Adames took the Giants' $182 million two winters ago, a toll that became the 32nd pick and the prep shortstop Brady Ebel, today the fourth-ranked prospect in their system.[^mccalvy] The succession at first base is already sketched: Andrew Vaughn, the right-handed half of the late platoon, enters his final year of arbitration, and the minors offer Blake Burke, 23, a left-handed hitter who struck 34 home runs between Biloxi and Nashville this past season.[^mccalvy] The method — the contract-year man exchanged for tomorrow, which yesterday's columns rehearsed in the catcher's context — has thus claimed its newest entry, and the question those columns weighed concerning William Contreras acquires a sharper edge this morning: Milwaukee has now lost the first baseman who handed its manager the final-out ball, and the telephone about the catcher has not stopped ringing.

news.subhead: THE EXCHANGE DESK: THE WRIGLEY MEN GO SHOPPING FOR A ROTATION ENTIRE AND KNOCK ON FIVE DOORS AT ONCE, BOSTON'S NEW PURCHASE CROWDS ITS OWN HOUSE, THE GULF COAST CLUB KEEPS ITS ACE AND LEAVES TWO OTHERS ON THE SHELF IN VIEW, AND MORE THAN HALF THE LEAGUE COMES CALLING FOR ONE LEFT ARM
news.body:
The Cubs' predicament, which these columns set out yesterday — a unanimous laureate in center field and not one incumbent starting pitcher — now has a shopping list attached. To the five free agents of the late rotation add the swingman Colin Rea, also at liberty, and Jameson Taillon, moved along in August: seven arms that made 121 starts for Chicago this past season, all gone, with Javier Assad the lone returning starter coming off a healthy year.[^roundup] The register of targets runs wide: Michael King, a pairing the MLB Network's man calls long forecasted; Kaima Taira, the Japanese right-hander who led his league with a 1.36 earned-run average over 146 innings, in whom Chicago's interest is reported strong; Freddy Peralta, whom Craig Counsell managed for years in Milwaukee and whom the Athletic's correspondent calls an obvious fit; Trevor Rogers; and Dustin May. The club is also said to want Clay Holmes and David Peterson back from its own departed shelf.[^roundup]

May, as it happens, is the winter's most democratically courted arm — the pitcher drawing the most interest at the meetings after Skubal himself, with the Cubs, White Sox, Padres, Astros and Marlins all in the circle. His 4.70 earned-run average across 145 and two-thirds innings for St. Louis and Milwaukee is no ornament, but the velocity has climbed back toward its early-career marks, his strikeout-minus-walk figure was a five-year best, and at 29 he is among the youngest starters at liberty.[^roundup] At Boston, meanwhile, the morning's lead item casts its shadow sideways: with Bauers installed and Contreras at first, the house is crowded, and the trade talk now turns on Jarren Duran — "clearly available," one National League evaluator says of the oft-rumored outfielder, though his cratered season and climbing wage complicate the return — and on the squeezed first baseman Triston Casas, whose accustomed stations are now doubly occupied.[^roundup] And on the Gulf Coast, the pennant-winners have sorted their rotation into the kept and the biddable: Erik Neander professes "every intention" of holding his ace Drew Rasmussen, whose $20 million option — the largest single-season wage in the franchise's books — was exercised last month, while the trade reports a deal involving Shane McClanahan or Ryan Pepiot a live possibility, both men lately acquainted with the surgeon and each a year or two from the open market.[^roundup]

The relief market, where the only actual ink of the meetings was spilled — Phillips, Pagán and Weiss, all chronicled in these columns this week — still holds its marquee names: David Bednar and Adrian Morejon, each dragging a qualifying offer behind him, with Raisel Iglesias and Kenley Jansen at liberty besides. In the Bronx the matter is declared urgent. "It's our main priority, to be honest," Brian Cashman says of his bullpen, two of whose three late-innings keepers — Bednar, tendered at $23.15 million, and Paul Blackburn — are free agents: "I am casting a wide net. We are asking around, and we need to find some stuff so we can feel good and sleep at night."[^hoch] The Yankees would have Morejon should Bednar walk, and would keep their left-hander Tim Hill — the same Hill the Mets are sniffing at, that club being linked to nearly every southpaw at liberty: Hill, Brooks Raley, A.J. Minter and Alex Vesia, the last of whom is reported to interest more than half the clubs in the league. One left arm, and a queue at the door sixteen clubs long at the least: the winter's arithmetic in miniature.[^roundup]

news.subhead: THE DUGOUT DESK: AUSMUS TAKES THE HOUSTON CHAIR WITH BAGWELL AND BIGGIO IN THE FRONT ROW — A FOUR-HOUR LUNCH AT SAN DIEGO SEALED THE MATCH, AND THE NEW MAN DECLINES ALL TALK OF GLORY DAYS
news.body:
The homecoming this paper recorded on Thursday was made ceremonial on Friday. Brad Ausmus was introduced as manager of the Astros at Daikin Park, with Jeff Bagwell and Craig Biggio, his old teammates, seated in the front row — and the story behind the hiring, told at last, turns out to have begun with a disappointment. Ausmus left the park on October 29 after interviewing for the general manager's position and told his wife, Liz, he did not expect to get it; he was right, Randy Flores being hired a day later. But Flores telephoned within days, offered to travel to San Diego, and the two men clicked over a four-hour lunch — Flores having first done his diligence through, among others, Aaron Boone, his college teammate and lately Ausmus's employer in the Yankee coaching rooms.[^mctaggart]

The introduction had its vaudeville — Flores, a pitcher in his playing days, asked from the dais whether Ausmus had owned him at the plate, and got back "I was 0-for-1 with a walk, and that's the truth" — but the new manager kept the sentiment on a short leash. "Looking back on my career, if I picture myself, it's wearing an Astros uniform," he said. "That being said, I'm not here to talk about the glory days. I'm here to talk about the Astros today, and the Astros going into 2027, which is now my main focus, and certainly the goal is to win the World Series." The work is considerable: a coaching staff to assemble, a bench coach first among the vacancies, and a roster that, for all the pleasure of writing the newly laureled Alvarez into the middle of its order, was swept from October's opening round and wants improving in several departments. Berkman and Oswalt have already rung with congratulations; the Herald suspects the congratulatory period will be brief.[^mctaggart]

news.subhead: THE FAR PACIFIC DESK: THE EASTBOUND TRAFFIC THICKENS — KOO, MOST VALUABLE OF THE KOREAN SERIES, ENGAGES AN AGENT TO TRY THE AMERICAN MARKET AT FOUR-AND-THIRTY
news.body: The procession across the Pacific, which brought Teruaki Sato's name to these columns on Tuesday and Kaima Taira's to the exchange desk above, now adds a Korean chapter. Ja-Wook Koo, the 33-year-old corner outfielder of the Samsung Lions — he turns 34 in February — has engaged Jaron Long of the Mako Corporation to explore a move to the Majors.[^greenspan] The credentials are a batting champion's: a .371 average this past season, the best in his league, with a .458 on-base mark, 15 home runs and 102 driven in across 114 games, his 1.039 OPS standing third among the circuit's qualified hitters; and when the Lions reached the Korean Series he batted .500 over the five-game set and was named its Most Valuable man. A left-handed hitter twelve seasons in the same uniform, he brings a career line of .322, which is the sort of number that travels well in any language. Where the younger Sato commands projections running toward nine figures, Koo's age makes him the value proposition of the eastbound register — and the Herald, which has watched this winter's market grow more international by the morning, adds his name to the watch list with pleasure.[^greenspan]

news.subhead: THE PROSPECT FIELDS: THE DESERT CROWNS ITS CHAMPION THIS EVENING — SURPRISE, SEVEN TIMES RUNNING A FINALIST, MEETS PEORIA FOR THE FALL LEAGUE TITLE BEHIND A SEMIFINAL IN WHICH ONE MAN DROVE HOME SEVEN
news.body:
The prospect calendar of 2026 closes this very evening. The Arizona Fall League, finishing school of the rising class, stages its championship game tonight at the Peoria Sports Complex, 8 o'clock Eastern on the MLB Network: the Surprise Saguaros, in the final for a seventh consecutive autumn, against the Peoria Javelinas, whom they beat for last year's title — the two clubs having posted the circuit's two best records besides.[^callis] The semifinals supplied their own theater. Cole Mathis, a first baseman in the Mets' chain, drove in seven runs — a Fall League playoff record — in Surprise's 10-4 dispatch of Glendale, while Peoria edged Salt River 6-5 on a decisive sacrifice fly from Ike Irish, the Orioles' young outfielder.[^callis]

The pitching assignment alone recommends the broadcast: Peoria sends Luke Holman of Cincinnati's system, who returned from elbow surgery to lead the league in earned-run average at 0.69 and hold the desert's hitters to a .114 average, against Justin Lamkin of the Kansas City chain. And whatever this evening decides, the autumn's breakout belongs already to Welbyn Francisca of Cleveland's system, who led the circuit in hitting at .427, in slugging, in OPS, in hits, in total bases and in runs driven in — a $1.375 million signing out of the Dominican Republic making a loud case for larger stages. The Herald commends the fixture to any reader whose scorecard hand has grown restless these sixteen gameless mornings.[^callis]

desk_note: A Saturday on which the winter found its voice. The silver season adjourned Thursday night; by Friday afternoon the market had produced its first great signature, as the lead column attests, and the desk observes that the sport allowed itself scarcely a night's repose between the last trophy and the first fortune. The forward ledger was ruled open before a word was written, per the house custom, and it stands as it stood: the camps' reporting dates are still to be posted, so the paper counts to the first rung with a date on it — the spring exhibition slate of Friday, the 19th of February, 97 mornings from this one, with Opening Night to follow 130 mornings off, on Wednesday, the 24th of March.[^bref] Nearer at hand, the desert plays its Fall League championship this very evening, as the prospect column records, and the 17th keeps its appointment three mornings hence — qualifying answers and silver bats together — though one answer, as the reader now knows, has already come back early and addressed to Boston. The collective agreement has 17 mornings left to live, and the week's dealings suggest the clubs intend to spend them busily. Until the morrow's dispatch, keep your scorecards near and your enthusiasms nearer.
